questiontext.text: In the Whole-Suite Evolution explorer, what does whole-suite generation do?

answer.text: It evolves an entire test suite at once so that the suite together maximises coverage of a chosen goal (all branches), rather than searching for one test at a time

feedback.text: Correct — the search optimises a whole suite toward covering every goal together.

answer.text: It searches for a single input vector that reaches one chosen target branch

feedback.text: That is single-branch targeting (the sbst-branch explorer); whole-suite generation optimises a whole suite for all goals.

answer.text: It measures the coverage of a fixed, hand-written suite without changing it

feedback.text: Whole-suite generation evolves the suite; it does not just measure a fixed one.

answer.text: It formally proves that the suite covers every reachable branch

feedback.text: It is a metaheuristic search that seeks coverage; it does not prove anything.

generalfeedback.text: Whole-suite generation (the EvoSuite idea) treats an entire test suite as one candidate and evolves it with a genetic algorithm so the suite as a whole covers all of the coverage goals, while keeping the suite small. This differs from targeting one branch with one evolving input vector.

questiontext.text: In this whole-suite genetic algorithm, what is a single individual (candidate) in the population?

answer.text: A whole test suite — a fixed-size set of test inputs evaluated together

feedback.text: Correct — each individual is an entire suite, not a single test.

answer.text: A single test input vector

feedback.text: In single-branch search an individual is one input vector; in whole-suite search it is a whole suite.

answer.text: One branch-outcome coverage goal

feedback.text: Goals are what the suite must cover; they are not the evolving individuals.

answer.text: The fitness value of the best suite so far

feedback.text: That is a score computed from an individual, not the individual itself.

generalfeedback.text: The defining move of whole-suite generation is that the unit of search is a suite. The GA holds a population of suites, scores each with a suite-level fitness, and evolves them with selection, crossover and mutation applied at the suite level.

name.text: The coverage goal of the search

questiontext.text: What coverage goal does the explorer drive the suite toward?

answer.text: Branch coverage — covering every branch of the target function, both outcomes

feedback.text: Correct — the gauge reads "Branch coverage" and the goals are the branch outcomes.

answer.text: Path coverage — covering every complete execution path

feedback.text: The explorer's goal set is branch outcomes, not whole paths.

answer.text: Mutation score — killing seeded mutants

feedback.text: Mutation testing is a different criterion; here the goal is branch coverage.

answer.text: Minimising running time of the suite

feedback.text: Speed is not the coverage goal; the goal is to cover all branches.

generalfeedback.text: The explorer optimises the suite for branch coverage: every branch contributes two goals (its true and its false outcome), and the suite is driven to cover all of them. The coverage gauge shows the percentage of those goals covered.

name.text: What counts as a coverage goal

questiontext.text: For branch coverage, what does the engine treat as a single coverage goal?

answer.text: One particular outcome of one branch — each branch yields two goals: taking it true and taking it false

feedback.text: Correct — every branch contributes a true-goal and a false-goal.

answer.text: One whole branch, counted once regardless of outcome

feedback.text: Each branch counts as two goals here, one per outcome.

answer.text: One test in the suite

feedback.text: Tests cover goals; a test is not itself a goal.

answer.text: One complete path through the function

feedback.text: Goals are branch outcomes, not paths.

generalfeedback.text: The engine's coverageGoals() lists, for every branch, both the true and the false outcome. So a function with b branches has 2b goals, and the suite must exercise each outcome at least once for full coverage.

name.text: Number of goals for a two-branch example

questiontext.text: Each example in the explorer has two branches. How many branch-outcome goals must the suite cover for 100%?

answer.text: 4 goals — two branches, two outcomes each

feedback.text: Correct — 2 branches, 2 outcomes each, gives 4 goals, as the "Covered: n / 4 goals" readout shows.

answer.text: 2 goals — one per branch

feedback.text: Each branch contributes two goals (true and false), so two branches give four.

answer.text: 8 goals — one per test in the suite

feedback.text: Goals come from branch outcomes, not from the four tests.

answer.text: 16 goals — one per individual in the population

feedback.text: The population size does not set the number of goals.

generalfeedback.text: With two branches, each having a true and a false outcome, there are 2 times 2 = 4 coverage goals. The tests panel reports coverage as "n / 4 goals", and 4/4 lights the full-coverage banner.

questiontext.text: By default, how many test inputs make up each candidate suite in the explorer? (Enter a number.)

feedback.text: Correct — the default suiteSize is 4, so the evolved suite panel lists four tests.

answer.text: four

feedback.text: Correct — four tests per suite.

generalfeedback.text: wholeSuiteGA runs with suiteSize 4, so each individual is a suite of four test inputs and the "Evolved suite" panel shows Test 1 through Test 4.

questiontext.text: What does the suite-level fitness add up across the goals?

answer.text: For each goal, the best (smallest) cost that any single test in the suite achieves toward that goal — summed over all goals

feedback.text: Correct — the per-goal contribution is the minimum test cost, summed over every goal.

answer.text: The cost of the first test only, ignoring the rest of the suite

feedback.text: Every goal takes the best across all tests, not just the first test.

answer.text: The total running time of all the tests

feedback.text: Fitness sums branch-distance costs, not run time.

answer.text: The number of tests in the suite

feedback.text: Suite size is a separate concern (minimisation), not the fitness sum.

generalfeedback.text: suiteFitness() walks every coverage goal, takes the minimum costForGoal over all tests in the suite (the closest any one test comes to that goal), and sums those minima. A lower sum means the suite as a whole is closer to covering everything.

questiontext.text: The suite-level fitness cost reaches 0 exactly when what is true?

answer.text: Every goal is covered by at least one test — full branch coverage

feedback.text: Correct — a zero sum means each goal's best cost is 0, so all goals are covered.

answer.text: Exactly one goal is covered

feedback.text: One covered goal zeroes only one term; the sum is zero only when all terms are zero.

answer.text: The suite has been reduced to a single test

feedback.text: Cost measures coverage distance, not suite size.

answer.text: The population has converged to identical suites

feedback.text: Convergence is unrelated to the cost being zero.

generalfeedback.text: Each goal contributes 0 to the sum precisely when some test covers it. The whole sum is 0 only when every goal is covered, which is full branch coverage — the point at which the explorer shows "Full branch coverage achieved."

questiontext.text: Besides maximising coverage, what second objective does whole-suite generation pursue?

answer.text: Minimising the suite's size — keeping the number of tests as small as possible for the coverage achieved

feedback.text: Correct — coverage is maximised while the suite is kept small.

answer.text: Maximising the number of tests, to be thorough

feedback.text: The aim is fewer tests, not more, for the same coverage.

answer.text: Maximising the branch distance of each test

feedback.text: Branch distance is minimised toward zero, and it is not the size objective.

answer.text: Maximising how long the search runs

feedback.text: Run length is a budget, not an objective.

generalfeedback.text: Whole-suite generation balances two goals: cover as much as possible and stay small. In the explorer, once full coverage is reached the "Minimised suite" panel drops redundant tests, showing the smaller suite that still covers everything.

questiontext.text: The "Minimised suite" panel says Redundant tests removed. Which tests does minimisation drop?

answer.text: Tests whose removal leaves the set of covered goals unchanged — they add no coverage the other tests do not already provide

feedback.text: Correct — a test is redundant if dropping it does not lose any covered goal.

answer.text: The slowest-running tests, regardless of coverage

feedback.text: Minimisation looks at coverage, not speed.

answer.text: Tests with the largest input values

feedback.text: Input magnitude is irrelevant; only coverage contribution matters.

answer.text: A fixed number of tests, always half the suite

feedback.text: The count removed depends on which tests are redundant, not a fixed fraction.

generalfeedback.text: minimiseSuite() checks each test: if the suite covers the same set of goals without it, that test is redundant and removed. The result is a smaller suite that still covers every goal the full suite did.

name.text: Why evolve a suite, not one test

questiontext.text: Why evolve a whole suite instead of running a separate single-test search once per goal?

answer.text: One suite-level search pushes toward all goals at once, and a single test often covers several goals as a side effect — so one run produces a small suite covering everything

feedback.text: Correct — the suite is optimised for all goals together, with collateral coverage along the way.

answer.text: Because a suite can cover goals that are individually impossible to reach

feedback.text: Infeasible goals stay infeasible; the benefit is optimising all reachable goals together.

answer.text: Because a suite needs no fitness function

feedback.text: The suite is guided by a suite-level fitness; it is not fitness-free.

answer.text: Because evolving a suite guarantees the minimum possible number of tests

feedback.text: Minimisation reduces size but does not guarantee a global minimum.

generalfeedback.text: Targeting one goal at a time can waste budget and ignores that a single test frequently satisfies several goals. Whole-suite generation optimises the entire suite against every goal simultaneously, then minimises, yielding a compact suite from a single search.

questiontext.text: The explorer displays "Full branch coverage achieved." What does that indicate about the suite?

answer.text: The coverage reading is 100% — every branch-outcome goal is covered by at least one test in the suite

feedback.text: Correct — the banner appears when coverage reaches 1 (all goals covered).

answer.text: Every test in the suite covers every goal

feedback.text: Full coverage needs each goal covered by some test, not every test covering every goal.

answer.text: The suite has been minimised to one test

feedback.text: The banner is about coverage, not the minimised size.

answer.text: No further generations are possible

feedback.text: The banner reflects coverage reached, not exhaustion of generations.

generalfeedback.text: The success banner shows when the current generation's best suite has coverage of 1 — all 4 goals covered. Suite cost is then 0, and the minimised-suite panel appears.

questiontext.text: How many candidate suites make up the population the genetic algorithm evolves?

answer.text: 16 suites

feedback.text: Correct — the explorer runs with populationSize 16.

answer.text: 4 suites

feedback.text: 4 is the number of tests per suite (suiteSize), not the population size.

answer.text: 1 suite

feedback.text: The GA evolves a population of suites, not a single one.

answer.text: 5000 suites

feedback.text: 5000 is the evaluation budget, not the number of suites per generation.

generalfeedback.text: wholeSuiteGA uses populationSize 16: sixteen suites per generation, evolved with tournament selection, crossover, mutation and elitism until the budget of 5000 evaluations runs out or full coverage is reached.

questiontext.text: What does the Run to end button do in the explorer?

answer.text: It jumps the view to the first generation at which the best suite reaches full coverage

feedback.text: Correct — it advances to the earliest fully-covering generation.

answer.text: It restarts the search from generation 1

feedback.text: That is Reset; Run to end jumps forward to full coverage.

answer.text: It re-runs the genetic algorithm with a new random seed

feedback.text: The seed is fixed at 1; Run to end only moves the view forward.

answer.text: It removes redundant tests from the current suite

feedback.text: Minimisation happens automatically once coverage is full; the button jumps the generation view.

generalfeedback.text: Run to end sets the displayed generation to the first one whose best suite has coverage of 1, so you can skip straight to the fully-covering result and its minimised suite.

questiontext.text: How is the coverage percentage on the gauge computed?

answer.text: Covered goals divided by total goals — e.g. 3 of 4 goals is 75%

feedback.text: Correct — coverage is covered divided by total goals.

answer.text: Covered goals divided by the number of tests in the suite

feedback.text: The denominator is the total goal count, not the suite size.

answer.text: The suite-level cost expressed as a percentage

feedback.text: Cost and coverage are related but distinct; coverage is a ratio of goals covered.

answer.text: The fraction of the evaluation budget used

feedback.text: Budget usage is unrelated to the coverage percentage.

generalfeedback.text: suiteFitness() returns coverage as covered divided by goals. With four goals, covering three gives 0.75, shown as 75% on the gauge; covering all four gives 100% and the full-coverage banner.

name.text: Why summing over all goals avoids per-branch bias

questiontext.text: Why does a suite-level fitness that sums the cost over all goals avoid the bias of a single-branch fitness?

answer.text: Because the single sum accounts for every goal at once, the search improves the suite wherever it is weakest instead of fixating on one chosen target branch

feedback.text: Correct — all goals enter one fitness, so no single branch dominates the search.

answer.text: Because summing removes the need for branch distance

feedback.text: Branch distance is still used inside each per-goal term; the sum just aggregates them.

answer.text: Because it weights the hardest branch to zero

feedback.text: No branch is zeroed out; every goal contributes its best-test cost.

answer.text: Because it ignores easy goals entirely

feedback.text: Easy goals are still summed in (contributing 0 once covered); none are ignored.

generalfeedback.text: Single-branch search commits its whole budget to one target. Whole-suite fitness folds every goal into one number, so progress on any uncovered goal lowers the fitness. The search is guided toward all goals together rather than biased toward a single branch.

questiontext.text: How does the whole-suite fitness differ from a single-branch fitness?

answer.text: It sums the branch-distance cost across all branch-outcome goals simultaneously, guiding one suite toward full coverage — unlike single-branch fitness, which targets one goal at a time

feedback.text: Correct — whole-suite fitness aggregates all goals; single-branch fitness handles one.

answer.text: It is identical to single-branch fitness; only the number of individuals evolved in parallel differs

feedback.text: The fitness itself differs: it aggregates all goals rather than one target.

answer.text: It assigns a random weight to each goal every generation to avoid overfitting

feedback.text: The goals are summed on equal footing; no random weighting is applied.

answer.text: It counts covered branches directly, so it is just a coverage percentage

feedback.text: It sums continuous branch distances, not a discrete covered-branch count.

generalfeedback.text: A single-branch fitness scores one input vector against one target branch. The whole-suite fitness scores an entire suite against every branch-outcome goal at once by summing each goal's best-test cost, so a single search drives the suite to full coverage.

questiontext.text: What is collateral coverage in whole-suite generation?

answer.text: A single test, while being driven toward one goal, incidentally covers other goals along its execution — so goals are covered for free

feedback.text: Correct — one test often satisfies several goals at once.

answer.text: Goals that can only be covered by combining two tests' executions

feedback.text: Coverage of a goal is per-test; collateral coverage is one test covering several goals.

answer.text: Coverage lost when a redundant test is removed

feedback.text: Minimisation removes tests without losing coverage; that is not collateral coverage.

answer.text: Extra branches added to the function during search

feedback.text: The function is fixed; collateral coverage is about goals covered as a side effect.

generalfeedback.text: Reaching a deep goal usually requires traversing earlier branches, so a test aimed at one goal frequently covers several others on the way. Whole-suite generation exploits this collateral coverage, which is why one suite can cover many goals without one test per goal.

questiontext.text: Whole-suite generation trades off two things. Which pair?

answer.text: Coverage (maximise) against suite size (minimise) — cover everything with as few tests as possible

feedback.text: Correct — high coverage with a small suite is the balance being struck.

answer.text: Branch distance against approach level

feedback.text: Those are the two components of one per-goal cost, not the suite-level trade-off.

answer.text: Population size against generation count

feedback.text: Those are GA parameters, not the coverage/size objective.

answer.text: Running time against memory use

feedback.text: The trade-off concerns coverage and suite size, not resource use.

generalfeedback.text: A bigger suite can cover more but is costlier to run and maintain. Whole-suite generation seeks maximum coverage with minimum size: it first drives coverage up, then minimises by removing redundant tests, giving a small suite that still covers everything.

name.text: Why the best per-goal cost is credited

questiontext.text: For each goal, the suite fitness takes the minimum cost over the suite's tests. Why the minimum rather than the average?

answer.text: A goal is covered if any single test reaches it, so only the closest test matters; averaging would penalise a suite for also containing tests aimed elsewhere

feedback.text: Correct — coverage is existential, so the best test per goal is what counts.

answer.text: The average is undefined when a goal is uncovered

feedback.text: The average is well-defined; the minimum is used because coverage needs only one test.

answer.text: The minimum is cheaper to compute than the average

feedback.text: The reason is semantic (existential coverage), not computational cost.

answer.text: Averaging would always give zero

feedback.text: Averaging would generally be positive; the point is that only one covering test is needed.

generalfeedback.text: A goal counts as covered when at least one test satisfies it. Crediting the minimum cost reflects that existential requirement: the suite is judged by its closest test to each goal. Averaging would wrongly punish a suite whose other tests target different goals.

name.text: Adding a test never lowers coverage

questiontext.text: Because each goal is credited to the best test in the suite, adding another test to a suite can never reduce the set of covered goals.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a new test can only match or improve each goal's best cost, so covered goals can only stay the same or increase.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Adding a test cannot worsen any goal's minimum cost, so coverage is monotone under adding tests.

generalfeedback.text: Each goal's contribution is the minimum cost over the tests. Adding a test can only lower or leave unchanged that minimum, so no covered goal is ever lost. This monotonicity is why minimisation works by removal: only redundant tests can go.

questiontext.text: When the explorer minimises the suite, what does it keep unchanged?

answer.text: The set of covered goals — the smaller suite covers exactly the goals the full suite covered

feedback.text: Correct — minimisation removes tests only if coverage is preserved.

answer.text: The number of tests in the suite

feedback.text: Minimisation reduces the test count; that is the point.

answer.text: The exact input values of every remaining test change

feedback.text: Remaining tests keep their inputs; only redundant tests are dropped.

answer.text: The order in which generations were explored

feedback.text: Generation history is unrelated to suite minimisation.

generalfeedback.text: minimiseSuite() removes a test only when the covered-goal set is the same without it. So the invariant preserved is the coverage achieved: the minimised suite covers precisely what the full suite did, using fewer tests.

questiontext.text: Which mapping of terms to roles is correct for whole-suite generation?

answer.text: Individual is a whole suite; goal is one branch outcome; suite fitness is the summed best-test cost over goals; minimisation drops redundant tests

feedback.text: Correct — each term maps to its whole-suite role.

answer.text: Individual is one branch outcome; goal is a whole suite; suite fitness is suite size; minimisation adds tests

feedback.text: These roles are swapped and wrong; minimisation removes tests, not adds them.

answer.text: Individual is one test input; goal is a path; suite fitness is running time; minimisation widens inputs

feedback.text: An individual is a suite, a goal is a branch outcome, and fitness sums branch distances.

answer.text: Individual is a mutant; goal is a seed; suite fitness is a mutation score; minimisation reseeds

feedback.text: These are mutation-testing terms, not whole-suite generation roles.

generalfeedback.text: In whole-suite generation an individual is an entire suite, a goal is a single branch outcome, the suite fitness is the sum over goals of each goal's best-test cost, and minimisation drops tests whose removal does not lose coverage.

name.text: Why not a raw coverage count as fitness

questiontext.text: Why does the suite fitness sum continuous branch distances rather than just counting how many goals are already covered?

answer.text: A raw covered-goal count is flat between coverings, giving the search no gradient; summed branch distances measure how close uncovered goals are and guide improvement

feedback.text: Correct — the continuous distance provides a gradient a discrete count lacks.

answer.text: A count would always equal the number of tests

feedback.text: The count equals covered goals, not tests; the real issue is the missing gradient.

answer.text: Branch distances are cheaper to compute than a count

feedback.text: The reason is search guidance, not computation cost.

answer.text: A count cannot reach full coverage

feedback.text: A count can reach full coverage; it just gives no guidance on the way there.

generalfeedback.text: Counting covered goals is a step function: it does not change until a goal flips from uncovered to covered, so the search has nothing to follow between steps. Summing branch distances makes near-misses score better than far-misses, giving the GA a smooth gradient toward coverage.

questiontext.text: When the explorer finishes on one of its examples, what does the evolved suite achieve?

answer.text: Full branch coverage — all four goals covered — after which redundant tests are removed to give a smaller suite

feedback.text: Correct — the examples reach 100% and then minimise.

answer.text: Coverage of the single target branch only

feedback.text: That is single-branch search; whole-suite generation covers all goals.

answer.text: A suite that always has exactly four tests after minimisation

feedback.text: Minimisation may leave fewer than four tests.

answer.text: A proof that no smaller suite exists

feedback.text: Minimisation is a heuristic removal, not a proof of minimality.

generalfeedback.text: On each example the search drives the best suite to full branch coverage (4/4 goals), lights the success banner, and then the minimised-suite panel shows the reduced suite after redundant tests are dropped.

questiontext.text: The whole-suite GA uses elitism. What does it do at the suite level?

answer.text: It carries the best suite of the current generation unchanged into the next, so the best coverage found is never lost

feedback.text: Correct — the elite suite survives to the next generation intact.

answer.text: It replaces the whole population with fresh random suites each generation

feedback.text: That would discard progress; elitism preserves the best suite.

answer.text: It mutates every test in the best suite before copying it

feedback.text: The elite is carried forward unchanged, not mutated.

answer.text: It removes the worst suite from the population

feedback.text: Elitism is about keeping the best, not deleting the worst.

generalfeedback.text: Elitism copies the current best suite straight into the next generation (and its cost is carried without re-evaluation). This guarantees the best coverage-so-far cannot regress as crossover and mutation explore new suites.

questiontext.text: How does crossover combine two parent suites in this GA?

answer.text: It splices the two suites at a cut point, taking some tests from one parent and the rest from the other to form a child suite

feedback.text: Correct — one-point crossover mixes whole tests between the two parent suites.

answer.text: It averages the numeric inputs of the two suites element by element

feedback.text: Crossover here recombines whole tests, not averaged numbers.

answer.text: It merges both suites into one twice-as-large suite

feedback.text: The child keeps the suite size; it does not grow.

answer.text: It swaps individual digits within a single test's number

feedback.text: The cut is between tests of the suite, not within a number.

generalfeedback.text: Suite-level crossover picks a cut index and concatenates the first parent's tests up to the cut with the second parent's tests after it, producing a child suite of the same size that inherits tests from both parents.

questiontext.text: How does mutation alter a suite in this GA?

answer.text: With a small probability per test, it replaces a test with a freshly generated random test, injecting new inputs into the suite

feedback.text: Correct — mutation swaps in a new random test now and then.

answer.text: It deletes a test from the suite, shrinking it

feedback.text: Mutation replaces rather than removes; suite size stays fixed until minimisation.

answer.text: It copies the best test over all the others

feedback.text: Mutation adds variety, not uniformity.

answer.text: It reorders the tests without changing their inputs

feedback.text: Reordering does not change coverage; mutation introduces new inputs.

generalfeedback.text: Suite mutation visits each test and, with probability 1/suiteSize, replaces it with a brand-new random test. This keeps injecting fresh inputs so the search can reach goals the current tests miss, while mostly preserving the suite.

questiontext.text: A generation's best suite shows "Covered: 3 / 4 goals" and the gauge reads 75%. What can you conclude?

answer.text: One branch outcome is still uncovered, so the suite cost is above zero and the full-coverage banner has not appeared

feedback.text: Correct — 3 of 4 goals means one outcome remains, cost above 0.

answer.text: Three of the four tests have been removed as redundant

feedback.text: 3/4 counts goals, not tests; minimisation only runs at full coverage.

answer.text: The suite cost is exactly 0.75

feedback.text: Coverage is 0.75, but the cost is the summed distance of the remaining uncovered goal, not 0.75 by definition.

answer.text: The search has failed and will stop

feedback.text: The search continues; later generations may reach the last goal.

generalfeedback.text: Coverage 3/4 is 75% and means one branch outcome is still uncovered. The suite's cost is therefore positive (the summed best-test distance to that last goal), and the "Full branch coverage achieved" banner and minimised-suite panel stay hidden until the last goal is covered.

name.text: Why one fitness for all goals

questiontext.text: Why fold every goal into a single suite fitness value rather than optimising goals one after another?

answer.text: A single fitness lets the GA improve the suite against all goals at once, so progress on any uncovered goal is rewarded and the whole search budget serves the whole suite

feedback.text: Correct — one aggregate fitness drives balanced progress across all goals.

answer.text: Optimising goals one after another is impossible

feedback.text: It is possible (that is per-goal search); the aggregate fitness is simply more efficient for whole suites.

answer.text: A single fitness makes each test cover every goal

feedback.text: Tests still cover different goals; the fitness just aggregates them.

answer.text: It removes the need for a population

feedback.text: The GA still evolves a population of suites.

generalfeedback.text: Aggregating all goals into one fitness means every generation's selection pressure improves the suite wherever it is weakest, and collateral coverage is captured automatically. Sequential per-goal optimisation would repeatedly restart and ignore that one test covers many goals.

name.text: Why summed branch distances beat boolean coverage

questiontext.text: Two suites each cover 2 of 4 goals but differ on the two uncovered goals: suite A's tests come very close to the missing outcomes; suite B's are far away. Why does the summed-branch-distance fitness prefer A?

answer.text: Both score the same on a boolean 2/4 count, but A's smaller summed distance to the uncovered goals gives a lower fitness, so the search follows the gradient toward covering them

feedback.text: Correct — the continuous sum distinguishes near-misses from far-misses that a count cannot.

answer.text: A covers more goals than B, so it obviously scores better

feedback.text: Both cover the same 2 goals; the difference is the distance to the uncovered ones.

answer.text: A has fewer tests than B

feedback.text: Size is not what the fitness compares here; it is the summed distance.

answer.text: The fitness prefers B, because larger distances explore more

feedback.text: Lower cost is better; the fitness prefers the smaller summed distance, which is A.

generalfeedback.text: A boolean covered-count is 2 for both suites and cannot rank them. The summed branch distance adds how far each uncovered goal is; A's near-misses sum to a smaller cost, so the GA prefers A and is steadily guided toward flipping those goals to covered.

name.text: Reading a coverage and cost combination

questiontext.text: Across generations the best suite's coverage rises from 50% to 100% while its suite cost falls to 0. What does the cost reaching 0 tell you that the coverage reading alone did not?

answer.text: Nothing extra at 100% — cost 0 and coverage 100% are equivalent — but during the climb the falling cost showed the suite getting closer to uncovered goals even while the coverage count was momentarily flat

feedback.text: Correct — at full coverage the two agree, but cost moves continuously between coverage steps.

answer.text: Cost 0 means the suite has exactly one test

feedback.text: Cost measures coverage distance, not suite size.

answer.text: Cost 0 means every test covers every goal

feedback.text: It means each goal is covered by some test, not every test.

answer.text: Cost 0 contradicts 100% coverage

feedback.text: They coincide: zero summed distance is exactly full coverage.

generalfeedback.text: At the endpoints cost 0 and coverage 100% say the same thing. The value of the cost is on the way there: it decreases continuously as tests approach uncovered goals, giving the search a gradient during the stretches where the discrete coverage count has not yet ticked up.

name.text: Collateral coverage in the nested guard

questiontext.text: In the nested-guard example, a test with x = 17 and y = 150 makes both branches true (b1 is x === 17, b2 is y greater than 100). Which goals does this one test cover?

answer.text: The true-outcome goals of both b1 and b2 — one test covers two goals as collateral coverage

feedback.text: Correct — reaching the inner true outcome also covers the outer branch's true outcome.

answer.text: Only the true-outcome goal of b2

feedback.text: To reach b2 the test must first take b1 true, so it covers that goal too.

answer.text: All four goals at once

feedback.text: The false outcomes of b1 and b2 need different inputs; one test cannot take a branch both ways.

answer.text: None, unless three more tests are added

feedback.text: This single test already covers two goals.

generalfeedback.text: x = 17 makes b1 true, and reaching b2 with y = 150 makes it true as well, so one test covers the b1-true and b2-true goals together. The two false-outcome goals require other inputs, illustrating why a small suite — not one test — is needed for full coverage.

name.text: Why minimisation runs after full coverage

questiontext.text: Why does the explorer minimise the suite only once full coverage is reached, not during the search?

answer.text: Minimisation removes tests that do not change the covered-goal set; doing it before full coverage could discard tests still needed as the search continues to close remaining goals

feedback.text: Correct — minimising the final covering suite is what yields a safe reduction.

answer.text: Because minimisation is what produces coverage in the first place

feedback.text: Coverage comes from the search; minimisation only trims the covering suite.

answer.text: Because minimisation increases coverage

feedback.text: Minimisation preserves coverage; it does not increase it.

answer.text: Because the population size must shrink first

feedback.text: Minimisation acts on the best suite's tests, not the population size.

generalfeedback.text: Minimisation is a post-processing step on the final covering suite: it drops tests whose removal keeps the covered-goal set intact. Applied mid-search it might remove tests whose coverage contribution only matters relative to the final suite, so the explorer waits until full coverage, then minimises.

name.text: Why the minimised suite may be smaller than four

questiontext.text: The evolved suite has four tests, but the minimised suite often has fewer. Why?

answer.text: Thanks to collateral coverage, a few tests can cover all four goals, leaving the others redundant — removable without losing any covered goal

feedback.text: Correct — overlapping coverage makes some tests redundant.

answer.text: Minimisation always halves the suite

feedback.text: The number removed depends on redundancy, not a fixed ratio.

answer.text: Some tests are deleted because they run too slowly

feedback.text: Removal is based on coverage redundancy, not speed.

answer.text: The four goals cannot all be covered, so tests are dropped

feedback.text: The examples do reach full coverage; redundant tests are what get dropped.

generalfeedback.text: Because a single test frequently covers several goals, the four evolved tests can cover the four goals with overlap. Any test whose goals are all also covered by the others is redundant and removed, so the minimised suite is often two or three tests.

questiontext.text: For a goal to count as covered by the suite, it is enough that at least one test in the suite takes that branch outcome.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — coverage of a goal is existential: one covering test suffices, which is why the fitness credits each goal's best test.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: A goal needs only one test to reach it; not all tests must.

generalfeedback.text: suiteFitness credits each goal with the minimum cost over the suite's tests, and a goal is covered when that minimum is 0 — i.e. some test reaches it. Coverage is existential over the suite, which underpins both collateral coverage and minimisation.

name.text: Covering a hard goal within a suite

questiontext.text: One goal in the multimodal example (x % 20 === 7 and x greater than 50) is hard to hit. In whole-suite generation, what must happen for that goal to be covered?

answer.text: Just one test in the suite must land on an input satisfying it; the other tests can pursue different goals

feedback.text: Correct — a single covering test in the suite is enough for that goal.

answer.text: Every test in the suite must satisfy it

feedback.text: Coverage is existential; only one test needs to reach the goal.

answer.text: The goal must be removed because it is too hard

feedback.text: Goals are not removed; the search keeps trying to cover them.

answer.text: Two tests must jointly execute it in one run

feedback.text: A goal is covered by a single test's execution, not two combined.

generalfeedback.text: Even for a hard goal, the suite covers it as soon as one of its tests hits a satisfying input. The suite fitness rewards the closest test to that goal, so mutation and crossover concentrate on nudging some test onto it while the rest of the suite handles the easier goals.

questiontext.text: Two suites both reach full coverage, so both have suite cost 0. How does whole-suite generation prefer one over the other?

answer.text: By size — the second objective is minimisation, so the smaller covering suite (after redundant tests are removed) is preferred

feedback.text: Correct — with coverage tied at full, fewer tests wins.

answer.text: By whichever was found in an earlier generation

feedback.text: Generation order is not the tie-breaker; suite size is.

answer.text: By larger input values, which are more thorough

feedback.text: Input magnitude does not decide preference; size does.

answer.text: They cannot be distinguished at all

feedback.text: They can: minimisation favours the smaller covering suite.

generalfeedback.text: Once coverage is tied at full (cost 0), the size objective breaks the tie. Minimisation strips redundant tests from the covering suite, and a suite that covers everything with fewer tests is the better result.

name.text: Approach level inside a per-goal cost

questiontext.text: In a per-goal cost within the suite fitness, what does the approach level term contribute?

answer.text: It counts how many required enclosing branches the test still failed to satisfy before diverging from the goal's path, added to the normalised branch distance at the divergence point

feedback.text: Correct — approach level plus normalised branch distance make up each per-goal cost.

answer.text: It counts how many tests in the suite are redundant

feedback.text: That is minimisation; approach level concerns one test's path to one goal.

answer.text: It is the number of goals still uncovered

feedback.text: Approach level is per-goal, per-test structural distance, not a global count.

answer.text: It is the suite's coverage percentage

feedback.text: Coverage percentage is a separate readout; approach level is inside a per-goal cost.

generalfeedback.text: costForGoal walks the goal's required branches; at the first one the test fails to satisfy, the approach level is how many required branches remain beyond it, and the normalised branch distance measures how close that decision came. Their sum is the per-goal cost, and the suite fitness sums the best such cost over all goals.

questiontext.text: Compared with running a separate single-branch search once per goal, what is the key advantage of whole-suite generation?

answer.text: A single search evolves one suite against all goals together, sharing budget and exploiting collateral coverage, and directly optimises the whole suite's coverage and size

feedback.text: Correct — one integrated search over the suite, not many isolated per-goal runs.

answer.text: It can cover goals that are individually infeasible

feedback.text: Infeasible goals remain uncovered either way; the gain is efficiency, not feasibility.

answer.text: It needs no fitness function at all

feedback.text: It uses a suite-level fitness; it is not fitness-free.

answer.text: It guarantees the globally smallest suite

feedback.text: Minimisation is heuristic; it does not guarantee global minimality.

generalfeedback.text: Per-goal search restarts for each target and ignores that one test can satisfy several goals. Whole-suite generation optimises the entire suite against every goal in one run, spends its budget across all goals, harvests collateral coverage, and jointly manages coverage and suite size.

questiontext.text: As you step through generations with Next, how do the best suite's cost and coverage typically move together?

answer.text: Cost trends down while coverage trends up (or holds), because elitism prevents the best suite from regressing, until cost hits 0 at full coverage

feedback.text: Correct — elitism makes the best suite non-worsening, so cost falls as coverage rises.

answer.text: Cost and coverage both rise together

feedback.text: Lower cost means better coverage; they move oppositely.

answer.text: Cost rises until coverage suddenly drops to 0

feedback.text: Elitism prevents the best suite from getting worse; cost does not climb.

answer.text: Both stay constant for the whole run

feedback.text: The search improves the best suite over generations; they change.

generalfeedback.text: Because the elite suite is carried forward, the best suite's cost never increases from one generation to the next. As tests approach and then cover goals, cost decreases and coverage increases, reaching cost 0 and 100% coverage at the fully-covering generation.

name.text: Effect of an unreachable goal on suite cost

questiontext.text: Suppose one branch outcome were infeasible (no input could ever take it). What would happen to the suite cost and coverage?

answer.text: That goal's best-test cost could never reach 0, so the suite cost would stay above 0 and coverage would plateau below 100%

feedback.text: Correct — an uncoverable goal leaves a permanent positive term in the sum.

answer.text: The suite cost would still reach 0 by covering the other goals

feedback.text: The sum includes the infeasible goal's positive cost, so it cannot reach 0.

answer.text: The infeasible goal would be automatically removed from the goal set

feedback.text: The engine does not drop goals; the term simply never zeroes.

answer.text: Coverage would still read 100%

feedback.text: Coverage counts covered goals; an uncovered one keeps it below 100%.

generalfeedback.text: The suite fitness sums every goal's best-test cost. An infeasible goal contributes a positive term no test can drive to 0, so the sum has a positive floor and coverage tops out below full — a useful signal that a goal may be unreachable (though the explorer's examples are all fully coverable).

name.text: Why suite fitness is not the sum of test costs

questiontext.text: Why is the suite fitness a sum over goals (best test per goal) rather than a sum over the suite's tests of each test's own cost?

answer.text: Coverage is a property of the suite as a whole: it matters that each goal is reached by some test, not that every individual test is good — summing per-test costs would reward redundancy and mis-rank suites

feedback.text: Correct — the goal-oriented sum measures what actually matters, whole-suite coverage.

answer.text: Per-test costs are impossible to compute

feedback.text: They are computable; they just do not measure suite coverage.

answer.text: Summing per-test costs always gives the same answer

feedback.text: It gives a different, coverage-blind answer that mis-ranks suites.

answer.text: A per-test sum would already equal the coverage percentage

feedback.text: It would not; it ignores whether each goal is covered by some test.

generalfeedback.text: What matters is that the suite covers every goal, so the fitness sums per goal the best test's cost. A per-test sum would penalise a suite for containing tests aimed at other goals and could favour many mediocre tests over a few that together cover everything.

name.text: Why one lucky test is not enough

questiontext.text: A suite contains one excellent test that covers three of the four goals, but the fourth goal stays uncovered by every test. What is the suite's status?

answer.text: Coverage is 75% and cost is positive — one strong test cannot substitute for covering the last goal, which needs some test to reach it

feedback.text: Correct — the fourth goal's positive term keeps cost above 0 and coverage below full.

answer.text: Coverage is 100%, because one test covering three goals is enough

feedback.text: The fourth goal is still uncovered, so coverage is not full.

answer.text: Cost is 0, because the best test is very good

feedback.text: Cost is a sum over goals; the uncovered goal keeps it positive.

answer.text: The suite is minimised to that one test

feedback.text: Minimisation only runs at full coverage, which has not been reached.

generalfeedback.text: The suite fitness sums each goal's best-test cost. Three covered goals contribute 0, but the fourth contributes its positive distance, so cost stays above 0 and coverage is 75%. Full coverage requires some test to reach that last goal, illustrating that whole-suite quality is about goals covered, not one test's brilliance.

name.text: What a minimised suite of N tests implies

questiontext.text: After minimisation the suite has N tests. What does that imply about each remaining test?

answer.text: Removing any one of them would drop at least one covered goal — each remaining test is needed to keep the covered-goal set intact

feedback.text: Correct — minimisation leaves only non-redundant tests.

answer.text: Each remaining test covers exactly one goal

feedback.text: A remaining test may cover several goals; it just must be non-redundant.

answer.text: N is guaranteed to be the smallest possible suite for full coverage

feedback.text: Greedy removal gives a non-redundant suite, not a proven global minimum.

answer.text: Each remaining test has a cost of 0 toward every goal

feedback.text: A test need only cover the goals it is responsible for, not all goals.

generalfeedback.text: Minimisation removes a test only when coverage is preserved without it, so once it stops, every remaining test is non-redundant: dropping it would lose a covered goal. This yields a minimal (in the removal sense) covering suite, though not necessarily the globally smallest one.
